readerValues.programmeDescription: Film and Literary Studies at Leiden examines how films and literary texts tell stories, create meaning and engage with society. Students practice close reading and film analysis, study historical movements and compare works across cultures and media. The program offers Film Studies and Literary Studies tracks. This record follows Film Studies, including film theory, documentary, digital cinema and a research thesis.
readerValues.comparisonExplanation: This qualified comparison relates the documented Film Studies curriculum to a full UCR program in literary, screen and visual interpretation. UCR offers sustained close analysis, adaptation, documentary and cultural research, with broader literary and media choices. Specialist film theory, repertories, animation, film-philosophy and digital-cinema depth remain differences; a complete Leiden degree pathway is not certified.

curriculum.limitation: The listed distinct components total 175 EC, including 30 EC of genuine open study. World Cinema is counted once; the additional 5 EC required allocation and future cohort sequencing remain unresolved. Full progression, specific minor access and graduation are not certified.

componentNotes.y1-lit-theory: Introduces literary concepts, theory and interpretation in relation to other media.
componentNotes.y1-text-image-1: Develops detailed analysis of narrative form, perspective, characters, space and time in prose and film.
componentNotes.y1-text-image-2: Extends analysis to poetic language and non-narrative or non-mainstream cinema.
componentNotes.y1-world-cinema-b: UCR offers cross-cultural and racial/media interpretation, but not the specified national-cinema repertories. Count this World Cinema component once.
componentNotes.y2-interculturality: Studies identity, difference and postcolonial approaches through cultural and literary objects.
componentNotes.y2-film-theory: Actual UCR film/adaptation and literary theories supply substantial critical approaches, but not the full specialist structuralist, apparatus, ideological and psychoanalytic film-theory sequence.
componentNotes.y2-cinema-postmodern: UCR analyzes intertextuality, medium specificity and representation; it does not supply this dedicated complex-cinema, cognitive/system and puzzle-film progression.
componentNotes.y2-paragone: Close visual, poetic and film-text work supports intermedial inquiry, but not the full word-image theoretical canon and video-essay workshop.
componentNotes.y2-documentary: Examines documentary representation in relation to evidence, truth, reality and ethics.
componentNotes.y3-film-philosophy: The selected program offers critical artistic interpretation, but not the specialized film-philosophy texts on perception, embodiment, time and whether film can think.
componentNotes.y3-cinema-digital: Material media histories and digital storytelling contribute, but not the dedicated digital-image, surveillance, VR, machine-vision and postproduction cinema inquiry.
componentNotes.thesis: Leiden requires a 10 EC individual film/literary thesis with its own entry, supervision and assessment. UCR course projects provide real research practice; optional 15 EC independent research is additional to its scheduled 180 EC, not compulsory thesis equivalence.
componentNotes.elective-space: 30 EC of genuine approved elective space. Duplicate-credit restrictions apply; no fixed subjects, unrestricted minor access or formally reconciled future placement is assumed.
componentNotes.y1-cinema-realism-modernism: UCR film history and documentary inquiry provide relevant foundations, but not this dedicated cinema realism/modernism movement-and-theory sequence.
componentNotes.y1-animation: Graphic narrative and media history contribute, but the selected program does not reproduce the dedicated comics, anime and animation history/conventions.
componentNotes.y2-digital-cultures: UCR television/digital narrative and media archaeology contribute distinct perspectives. The wider humanities transformation through generative AI, Big Tech and digital research is not a dedicated sequence here.
componentNotes.y2-philosophy-science: Qualitative inquiry and critical interpretation develop methodological reflection; the dedicated philosophy-of-science and humanities framework remains distinct.
componentNotes.y3-third-cinema: Racial, postcolonial and environmental media inquiry provides political-cultural connections; Latin American Third Cinema and its specific non-Western film-theoretical tradition remain distinct.

cellNotes.text: Both develop close literary interpretation and core narrative/form concepts. UCR includes applied criticism across several genres; the exact theoretical canon and historical organization differ.
Both interpret literary form in historical context. UCR surveys works from ancient epic to later fiction; it does not reproduce the dedicated Realism, Naturalism and Symbolism sequence.

Both examine narration, point of view and textual choices through precise analysis. UCR develops linguistic stylistics chiefly in written texts; the integrated prose-and-film analysis remains broader at Leiden.
Both analyze poetic form, sound, rhythm and meaning. UCR combines close reading with composition and performance; the dedicated non-narrative and non-mainstream cinema strand remains distinct.
Both compare narratives across cultures and periods using close reading and contextual interpretation. UCR emphasizes myth, transmission and adaptation; Leiden’s wider world-literary corpus differs.

Both analyze how texts, films and cultural forms shape public understanding of current issues. UCR concentrates on climate communication; Leiden’s range also includes migration, precarity, fascism, heritage and AI.

Both compare literary and film narrative through close analysis, medium specificity and adaptation theory. UCR develops sustained text-film research; Leiden additionally treats broader transmedia worlds and fan/consumer participation.

Both examine documentary representation, authenticity, evidence and ethical or aesthetic choices. UCR adds documentary production; the precise theoretical cases and audiovisual-evidence emphasis differ.

Both analyze cinematic form, narrative conventions and film history. UCR also studies television/digital media and feminist/postcolonial interpretation; Leiden provides a dedicated sequence of genre case studies.

Both develop a research question, analyze evidence and explain methods and findings. UCR supplies qualitative, documentary and visual inquiry; it does not replace the dedicated film-and-literary research workshop.

Both examine colonial legacies, cultural representation and interpretive position. UCR focuses on African art, diaspora and heritage; Leiden’s postcolonial literary/film theory and wider identity concepts are not fully reproduced.

Both analyze cultural objects and institutions as representations shaped by meaning, identity and ideology. UCR concentrates on modern/global art, museums and reception; Leiden ranges more broadly across media and historical periods.
